title: Sam Presti Reflects on Russell Westbrook's Retirement
htmlContent:
Mid-August is usually the quietest stretch on the NBA calendar. Free agency has settled, training camps are weeks away, and most front offices are catching their breath. For the Oklahoma City Thunder, Aug. 12 turned out to be anything but ordinary.

That was the day Russell Westbrook announced his retirement. After 18 seasons, one of the defining superstars of the 2010s shared the news on social media through a video narrated by actor Michael B. Jordan, a fittingly dramatic exit in which Westbrook himself never said a word. For Thunder fans, it closed the book on the player who, more than almost anyone, helped turn a relocated franchise into a perennial contender.

Westbrook's all-out style drew plenty of critics over the years. Few players split opinion quite like he did. But few players were ever as impossible to ignore, and his announcement produced the kind of moment basketball fans tend to remember exactly where they were for.

Where Sam Presti Was When He Heard

Thunder general manager Sam Presti was about as far from Oklahoma City as he could be. Speaking at his preseason press conference ahead of the 2026–27 season, Presti explained that he had taken his family to Italy for the summer, partly to explore ancestry on his father's side. The news broke on the final night of the trip, while the family was riding back in a van from an outing his wife had planned.

Presti doesn't use social media, so he relies on the Thunder's public relations staff to keep him current, usually by way of screenshots. That is how the news reached him. He said he went quiet, admitting that it hit him pretty hard and that he simply hadn't seen it coming.

A Career That Rewrote the Record Book

It is easy to see why the moment landed so heavily. Westbrook retires as the NBA's all-time leader in triple-doubles with 209. He also owns the single-season record of 42, set during his 2016–17 MVP campaign, when he became the first player since Oscar Robertson to average a triple-double over a full season.

The rest of the résumé is just as imposing: nine All-Star selections, two scoring titles, three assist titles, back-to-back All-Star Game MVP awards, an Olympic gold medal in 2012, and a place on the NBA's 75th Anniversary Team. He spent his first 11 seasons with the Thunder, became the franchise's leader in most major statistical categories, and finished his career last season with the Sacramento Kings.

No matter where he played after leaving Oklahoma City, his identity never really changed. Westbrook will be remembered first and foremost as a member of the Thunder.

The Draft Pick Nobody Else Saw Coming

That legacy began with a gamble. In the 2008 NBA Draft, the franchise—then still the Seattle SuperSonics before relocating that summer—used the No. 4 overall pick on Westbrook. At UCLA he had been known as a raw, defense-first guard, and many analysts considered the selection one of the biggest reaches of the draft. History has been unkind to those critics.

Presti remembers the road to that pick well. Westbrook's first workout with the team ended early when he got hurt partway through, in a session Presti believes also included George Hill. The Thunder kept asking for another look, but Westbrook's camp had a back injury to manage and assumed he would be drafted much later, so they declined. Presti also kept quiet about how seriously the team was considering him at No. 4.

The Hotel Room Meeting That Sealed It

For Presti, the push for more time with Westbrook was never really about his jump shot or his athleticism. He already liked the player. What he wanted to know was the person: whether Westbrook had the mental toughness and intangibles that separate franchise-changing picks from talented ones.

A sit-down in an Orlando hotel room answered that question. Westbrook's responses confirmed what Presti's instincts had been telling him, that this was someone capable of carrying a franchise. Over the next 11 seasons, Westbrook became a co-star on the team's first true title contender and a centerpiece of the organization's identity.

A Full-Circle Moment

Roughly an hour after the news reached him in Italy, Presti's phone rang. It was Westbrook. The two had a long conversation, looked back on their years together, and Presti joked that remembering their first workout made him feel old.

He described the retirement as such a full-circle moment for a player and person who had shaped so much of the franchise's history. In the team's official statement, he called Westbrook "the ultimate competitor," and at his press conference he said he was simply happy for him. Presti said he was confident the qualities that made Westbrook great on the court will carry into whatever comes next.

The Thunder have since reached the league's summit, winning the 2025 NBA championship with a new core. But the foundation of that organization was laid years earlier by a fearless guard from UCLA whom few others were willing to bet on. On Aug. 12, that chapter officially came to a close.
excerpt: Thunder general manager Sam Presti was in Italy with his family when Russell Westbrook's retirement announcement reached him on Aug. 12, closing the book on the player who helped transform the franchise into a perennial contender over 11 defining seasons.
